web_evidence.title: Gods and generals / by Jeff Shaara — Cherry Hill Public Library catalog
web_evidence.note: The library-hosted, rights-cleared Antietam/Sharpsburg excerpt sustains external narration of Chamberlain as “he,” while clearly marking first-person language as speech or thought.

web_evidence.title: Jeffrey Shaara Writing Styles in Gods and Generals
web_evidence.note: The point-of-view section explicitly identifies third-person narration throughout, explaining that focalization rotates among Lee, Jackson, Hancock, Chamberlain, and a few secondary characters without changing to first person.

web_evidence.title: Gods and Generals Teacher’s Guide — Random House Academic Resources
web_evidence.note: The publisher’s guide describes four character-headed parts and alternating focal viewpoints across the novel; its discussion and quoted narrative passages consistently treat those focal characters externally, corroborating rotation within third person rather than person alternation.

person_note: The controlling narration is third person with rotating focal characters, not alternating grammatical persons. Quotes q00002, q00006, and q00007 independently show external scene narration, and the sustained library excerpt reproduces the same pattern. The first-person language in q00002 is explicitly introduced as thought; the many dialogue quotes are local speech. Q00004’s unattributed “I” is likewise local character material or a quote-boundary error because the whole-book analysis states that even character-focused chapters remain third person. The publisher guide confirms that the book alternates focal viewpoints among character-headed chapters, while BookRags explicitly confirms that those chapters do not switch to first person. The only minor uncertainty is the missing local context for q00004, not the book-level person.
